newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's Transgas plans to expand natgas network.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's Transgas plans to expand natgas network.

text.p: State gas company Transgas said it planned to expand its distribution network in central Portugal following the inauguration of a $1.88 billion pipeline carrying natural gas from Algeria.

"The board of Transgas will propose, at the general assembly of shareholders in March, the inclusion in its medium term plan for 1997/99 of the enlargement of the concession area to the districts of Viseu, Guarda, Castelo Branco and Portalegre," according to a company document made available to Reuters.
The pipeline, inaugurated last week, transports natural gas from Algeria via Morocco and Spain to Portugal.
Domestic consumers in Portugal will have to wait some two months before receiving the natural gas due to delays in setting up the regional distribution network, a Transgas source said.
The Transgas general assembly will take place on March 27, the source added.
No estimates for the cost of the expansion of the natural gas network in central Portugal were immediately available.
The Transgas document projected that Portugal would receive 2,231 million cubic metres of natural gas in 1999 and 2,846 million cubic metres in 2003.
Portugal received no natural gas supplies before the construction of the pipeline was completed last November, a Transgas spokesman said.

The Transgas document said that Portugal planned to acquire a "complementary supply" of up to 500 million cubic metres of liquefied natural gas from Nigeria, via a terminal at Huelva in southern Spain, from 1999.
Last week Nigeria LNG, a unit of Royal Dutch/Shell Group, denied a Portuguese newspaper report that it was in talks to sell natural gas to Transgas.

The document also said it was possible that Transgas would acquire from 1998 an emergency supply of natural gas or liquefied natural gas from a European company of up to 500 million cubic metres per month.
It said that Transgas planned to establish underground reserves of natural gas in the district of Pombal in central Portugal from 1999.
The document said that the arrival of the Algerian natural gas in Portugal would diversify energy supplies and provide 10 percent of the consumption of primary energy in the country.
It would reduce emissions of sulphur dioxide to the atmosphere by 30 percent and carbon dioxide by five percent.

The natural gas will reduce prices paid by domestic consumers by between 20 and 65 percent, industrial consumers by between three and 40 percent and electrical producers by more than 10 percent, the document said.
